tiers.featured: Featured products: full narrative case studies.
tiers.technical: Technical projects: shipped systems from professional work.
tiers.experiments: Experiments: smaller explorations, prototypes and learning projects. Status labels are honest; nothing here is presented as shipped unless it is.

projects.name: ReadTrail
projects.statusLabel: Working MVP, 2.0 on main and unreleased; not yet on the Chrome Web Store
projects.tagline: A privacy-first Chrome reading companion: follow the line, keep your exact place, and write beside the passages you saved.
projects.idea: ReadTrail helps people read long, text-heavy material in Chrome without losing their place, then keep the passages that mattered and write with them, with every quote still able to go back to its paragraph.
projects.problem: Dense text makes it easy to lose the current line, forget where you stopped, or abandon unfinished reading because returning takes too much effort. And for people who read to answer a question, what they gather loses its connection to where it came from: a saved highlight is an orphan a month later, with no reliable way back to the exact paragraph.
projects.question: How can a browser help people continue reading without turning their attention into another data stream?
corePromise: Follow the text while actively reading.
Stop without worrying about losing the exact reading position.
Return later and continue with minimal effort.

principles.title: Reading comes first
principles.text: Quiet and lightweight. It supports attention without becoming another interface the reader has to manage.

principles.title: The browser is the natural home
principles.text: Built into the environment where the reading already happens: a side panel beside the page, not a separate reading app.

principles.title: Use is intentional
principles.text: Opt-in per page. No reading state is collected before the reader turns it on for that page in that tab.

principles.title: Memory should be trustworthy
principles.text: When it says it remembers a position, the reader can rely on it. When it cannot find something, it says so instead of guessing.

principles.title: Privacy is part of the product
principles.text: Reading history reveals sensitive interests. Everything stays on the device, saving is always an explicit choice, and incognito tabs leave nothing durable.

principles.title: Grow from position to understanding
principles.text: Exact position is the foundation. Passages, notes and drafts were built on top of it, and the only relation between two sources is one the reader wrote: quoting both in one draft.

notList: An automatic surveillance log of browsing activity
A read-it-later dumping ground with no sense of position
A productivity dashboard that judges how much someone reads
A replacement for the browser or the original page

coreFlow.text: Click the toolbar icon to open the side panel and turn ReadTrail on for this page. The panel warns first: while it is on, clicks pause and resume reading instead of opening links.
A ruler, underline or dots follows the line you are reading, spanning only the text it is on.
One click pauses the marker on a line, anchored to the text so it stays attached while scrolling. Click again to resume.

An explicit choice in the side panel: one durable resume point per exact URL. If a tab closes with unsaved progress, the panel's Recently closed list offers to keep it (or a setting always or never saves).
Select text and choose Save selection in the panel, or Save selection to ReadTrail from the right-click menu. The clip keeps its page, title and exact position, and the kept text flashes to confirm.

A full tab with your sources on the left and a draft on the right. Quote a passage and it keeps its citation. Return goes back to that paragraph and says whether it found it exactly, found it by its wording because the page changed, or did not find it.
Copy the draft as Markdown or download a .md file: quotes become blockquotes with numbered references, and a Sources list gives each page once.
Library, then Pages, in the side panel opens a saved page, turns ReadTrail on and restores the position. If the page changed since you saved, it says so.

states.name: Following
states.text: Light, translucent guide. Responsive but quiet.

states.name: Paused
states.text: Stronger fixed treatment for the temporary checkpoint, aligned to the visual centre of the line.

states.name: Saved
states.text: Warm-gold band with dashed edges and a left edge flag for a deliberate save. Distinguishable without relying on colour alone.

decisions.decision: Opt-in per page, dormant by default
decisions.tradeoff: The content script is injected on every http(s) page but stays inert: until the reader turns it on it registers no event listeners, draws nothing, records no position and writes no state. On-demand injection was rejected because side-panel clicks do not grant activeTab and Continue reading opens tabs programmatically. An end-to-end test checks a fresh page is dormant.

decisions.decision: Page text is read only when the reader asks
decisions.tradeoff: This replaced the 1.0 rule 'store only what restores a position' once passages and drafts arrived. Save selection reads the selection and stores it; Return reads the page to find a saved passage and keeps nothing it sees. A third read needs the owner's decision. Position anchors still contain no page text.

decisions.decision: Active ReadTrail is an explicit reading lock
decisions.tradeoff: Primary clicks pause or resume instead of activating links and buttons. Scrolling and text selection stay available. Reading loses some page interactivity, but the pause gesture works even on linked text.

decisions.decision: The side panel replaces the popup and Reading Space
decisions.tradeoff: One entry point beside the page, at the cost of requiring Chrome 114. Playwright cannot drive the real docked panel, so that surface stays on a manual checklist.

decisions.decision: Reading state is kept per tab, validated by URL
decisions.tradeoff: URL-keyed state produced cross-tab activation, orphaned reading locks and lost updates. Per-tab records fix that, at the cost of cleanup on tab close and a stricter sender-based trust rule.

decisions.decision: Never add the tabs permission
decisions.tradeoff: It would add a browsing-history install warning. Without it the worker cannot see tab URLs, so it asks the content script, and Return can reuse only a tab the reader already saved a clip from.

decisions.decision: Relations are quotations, not inferences
decisions.tradeoff: Two sources are related because the reader quoted both in one draft. Automatic connections by shared tag or domain were retired and their module deleted: less to discover, nothing the reader did not author.

decisions.decision: Return never claims more than it knows
decisions.tradeoff: Resolving both anchors is not enough to report 'found exactly': the resolved text must equal the stored clip text. Otherwise it searches by wording and reports approximate, or missing. Slower to say yes, never wrong about it.

decisions.decision: Permanent saving is a separate decision
decisions.tradeoff: Temporary progress never silently becomes history. Saving is an explicit Save for later; a closing tab is offered through a quiet Recently closed list rather than a notification, so no extra permission is needed.

decisions.decision: One automatic position, many intentional bookmarks
decisions.tradeoff: Keeps the mental model simple: the trail remembers where you stopped; you decide what is worth marking. Bookmarks are still not built; double click is reserved for them.

decisions.decision: Document planned work separately from shipped work
decisions.tradeoff: The README's roadmap is explicitly 'planned work, not completed claims', and decisions go in an append-only, numbered log (97 so far). Slower-looking, but honest.

stack: Chrome Extension (Manifest V3), Chrome 114 or newer
Plain JavaScript, HTML, CSS: no bundler, no runtime dependencies
Chrome Side Panel API for page controls and the library
Canvas overlay for the reading guide
CSS Custom Highlight API for saved passages, Return's flash and the line highlight (no DOM changes to the page)
chrome.storage.session for per-tab temporary state
chrome.storage.local for preferences, saved places, passages, notes, tags and drafts
Vitest + JSDOM (394 unit and behavioral tests in 15 files)
Playwright (11 end-to-end scenarios against the unpacked extension in Chromium)

modules.name: background/service-worker.js
modules.role: The single trust boundary. Validates every message and stored record, owns every durable write, keeps per-tab state, the Recently closed list and Continue reading.

modules.name: background/library.js
modules.role: Knowledge-layer handlers (passages, notes, page tags, drafts, export and import) and the Save selection to ReadTrail context menu, which confirms a save on the page or marks that tab's icon when it fails.

modules.name: shared/
modules.role: Constants, error codes, validators and the page-controls state machine, loaded by every surface.

modules.name: content/position.js
modules.role: Finds the readable line and builds an anchor: a node path and offset, a nearby landmark id and a structural check, plus scroll offsets. No page text.

modules.name: content/renderer.js
modules.role: Canvas rendering of following, paused and saved states in ruler, underline or dots style.

modules.name: content/content.js
modules.role: Page lifecycle: activation, reading lock, click handling, restoration and the line highlight.

modules.name: content/passage.js
modules.role: Captures the selection only on request, draws saved passages with CSS highlights, and resolves or searches for a passage when the reader presses Return.

modules.name: sidepanel/
modules.role: The side panel: this-page controls, Recently closed, Library (Pages and Tags), search, and import, export and clear.

modules.name: sidepanel/desk.html
modules.role: The Desk, its own full-tab document: sources beside drafts, quotes, Return, and Markdown export.

modules.name: options/
modules.role: Appearance, closing-tab behaviour and excluded sites, written only through the worker.

architecture.dataModel: Session (cleared with the browser): readtrail.tab.v1:<tabId> = { url, title, active, mode, position, incognito, origin, restoreQuality? }; readtrail.recent.v1 = { items: [{ tabId, url, title, position, closedAt }] } (max 10, 30 minutes); readtrail.seen.v1:<tabId> = { url } (written when a clip is saved from that tab). Local (this device only): settings; readtrail.saved.v1:<exactUrl> = { title, position, savedAt }; readtrail.passage.v1:<uuid> = { url, title, text (up to 4,000 characters), start, end, note, tags }; readtrail.note.v1:<uuid> = { url, title, text, tags }; readtrail.pagemeta.v1:<url> = { tags }; readtrail.draft.v1:<uuid> = { title, tags, blocks: [ { type: text, text } | { type: quote, passageId, text, url, title } ] }. Version, id and timestamp fields omitted here; storage.sync is never used.
keyIdeas: Tab identity comes from the sender: a content script's tab is sender.tab.id and any tabId it sends is ignored; only an extension page may name a tabId; a tab record counts only when its URL matches.
A durable record about a page must be attributable to a tab, so incognito is refused at the worker, and the panel never offers a save it would refuse.
Durable writes are bounded: 1,500 passages and notes, drafts capped at 100, and any new write refused past 9 MB. Removals, clearing and settings are never refused.
Import in replace mode writes the new records before removing the old ones, and cross-checks every quote against its passage so a file cannot fabricate a source.
The content script is declared on all http(s) sites but stays inert until activated; that dormancy is the main permission justification, and a test proves it.

projects.whereAIFits: Not in the product yet, by choice. 1.0 and 2.0 make no network requests at all, so the first store review carries no third-party data disclosure. Planned for 1.1: optional AI actions (summaries, tag and connection suggestions) using the reader's own Anthropic key, off unless a key is added, acting on a draft and never on a live page. It stays owner-gated and has not started.
projects.process: Built with a review-led agent workflow. Priyanshu owns the product vision, resolves product questions and approves every push and tag. Claude Code is the lead (sprint scope, implementation, tests, and the only committer); Codex independently reviews each phase diff and drives browser QA; an OpenCode worker takes one bounded task in named files and cannot commit. Ten sprint documents carry scope and acceptance criteria. Sprint 010 ran as three parallel sessions on separate branches, each reviewed and merged by the lead, who fixed two defects the sessions reported.
shipped: Reading guide (ruler, underline or dots) following the current line, spanning only the text it is on
Reading lock: one click pauses at a line, anchored to the text while scrolling; another click resumes
Appearance settings (style, colour, size, opacity, line highlight), closing-tab behaviour and excluded sites
Side panel, replacing the popup and Reading Space: this-page controls, Recently closed, and Library with Pages and Tags
Explicit Save for later, one durable resume point per exact URL; Continue reading restores it and says when the page changed
Per-tab reading state: two tabs on the same page never share activation, position or reading lock
More resilient restoration: landmark anchors, structural checks and a proportional fallback
Recently closed: an offer to keep a tab that closed with unsaved progress (ask, always or never)
Passages (Save selection in the panel or the right-click menu), notes, page tags, local search grouped by page, JSON export and import
The Desk: drafts beside your sources, quotes that keep their citation, and Return to the exact paragraph with an honest verdict
Markdown out: Copy as Markdown, Download .md and Copy with source, with numbered references and a Sources list
The Desk as one document: Enter, Backspace, Up and Down move across blocks, quotes are embeds the caret steps over, and blocks drag by a handle
A right-click save that confirms itself: the kept text flashes, and a failure shows '!' on that tab's icon with the reason
Two scoped clears, Clear saved places and Clear page content, each confirmed first; neither touches drafts or settings
Incognito: the guide works, nothing durable is stored and no save is offered
No account, sync, analytics or network requests
394 unit and behavioral tests (Vitest, 15 files) and 11 Playwright end-to-end scenarios
roadmap: Submit 2.0.0 to the Chrome Web Store (1.0.0 was completed but never submitted)
Text-only PDF clips through the right-click menu (Sprint 011), after checking Chrome's PDF viewer in a real browser; Return on a PDF quote will say plainly it cannot locate the passage
A fifth design critique of the Desk: if flexibility still scores 1, the editor is redesigned again before anything else
A keyboard shortcut for Save selection, and tag autocomplete
First-run and empty states that show one next action
Manual QA in a real Chrome for touch, IME, a screen reader and narrow-column articles, which no automated run covers
1.1: optional AI actions with the reader's own Anthropic key, off unless a key is added
openQuestions: Nobody outside the project has used ReadTrail on a real page yet. What will the first two or three students or writers stumble on?
What is the simplest activation gesture that feels native to the browser?
How precise must restoration be when a page changes between visits?
When does an unfinished item become completed?
What does 'contributed to my knowledge' mean from the reader's point of view?
Which knowledge features genuinely improve reading rather than create collection overhead?
whatItShows: Product thinking: decisions, non-goals and open questions are written down and separated, and 97 numbered decisions record why things changed
Honesty as a feature: Return reports exact, approximate or missing, and the docs record fixes that passed their tests and were still wrong
UX judgment: three guide states told apart without colour alone, reduced motion in the panel and on Return's scroll, and a keyboard path beside the drag handle
System design: one trust boundary, per-tab state, provenance checks on import, bounded storage
Privacy as architecture: dormant by default, two explicit reads, no network, no tabs permission
Curiosity: a real problem from his own reading habit

projects.name: Priyanshu OS / AI Voice Portfolio
projects.statusLabel: Working MVP: deployed on its own domain, and you are reading it
projects.tagline: A portfolio you talk to. An AI agent grounded in structured profile data that can answer, navigate and reason about fit.
projects.idea: Replace the static resume with an agent that answers questions about Priyanshu's background, navigates this site, surfaces relevant work, and analyses a pasted job description against his actual experience.
projects.problem: Resumes flatten a non-linear path into bullet points. Recruiters and hiring managers have specific questions, and a static page cannot answer them or admit what it does not know.

principles.title: Grounded, not generative
principles.text: Every answer derives from /data/*.json. The agent is instructed to say when something is not in the data rather than fill the gap.

principles.title: Gaps are a feature
principles.text: The relevance mode reports missing experience explicitly. A match list without gaps is not trustworthy.

principles.title: Actions over prose
principles.text: The agent can navigate the page and highlight dimensions through tool calls, so an answer is also a demonstration.

stack: Next.js 15 (App Router) and TypeScript, Tailwind v4, self-hosted OFL fonts
Up to four OpenAI-compatible providers tried in order, now Gemini, OpenRouter and Groq (Cerebras led until its free tier ended in 2026), with a five-minute circuit breaker and a per-attempt timeout
Per-provider prompt sizing: a provider with a smaller token allowance is sent a smaller knowledge base
Structured JSON output for UI actions, validated against known section, dimension and project ids before anything runs
In-memory rate limiting on both model routes, with the daily provider budget split between them
Web Speech API for voice in and out, d3-force for the knowledge graph, Motion for one authored motion grammar

projects.whereAIFits: Central. This is a tool-using agent with grounding, structured outputs and explicit gap reporting. Its limits are also documented: no persistent memory, browser-native voice quality, and dependence on free-tier model rate limits.

screenshots.alt: The portfolio homepage: a career plotted as Fig. 1 on quadrille paper, with an ask input drawn as an annotation on the plot
screenshots.caption: The career as a plotted function, with the ask input drawn as an annotation on it

screenshots.alt: The marginalia panel open beside the figure, answering whether he is primarily technical or business
screenshots.caption: The agent answers in the margin, grounded in the same JSON the page renders from

screenshots.caption: A pasted job description, an honest verdict, and matches that cite their source row

coreFlow.text: Fig. 1 plots the career as a curve. The ask input is drawn on the plot as an annotation, not bolted on as a chat bubble.
The question goes to a system prompt built from the same six JSON files the page itself renders from.
The reply arrives in the margin, in third person, and says plainly when something is not on record.
Validated actions move the page: scroll to a section, hatch the relevant tracks, open a case study.
Paste a job description. Every claimed match must cite a dataset id, and an uncited one is dropped rather than shown.
Missing experience comes back as output, next to the matches, instead of being left out.

decisions.decision: The data is the source of truth, not the components
decisions.tradeoff: Every section and every AI answer renders from six JSON files, so the page and the agent can never disagree. A copy fix needs a deploy, which is the price of there being one version of the truth.

decisions.decision: Grounded, not generative
decisions.tradeoff: The prompt forbids invention and requires "that is not something I have on record". It refuses questions a looser agent would happily answer, which is the point: a portfolio agent that guesses is worse than no agent.

decisions.decision: Gaps are output, not omission
decisions.tradeoff: The fit check returns missing experience alongside the matches, so the site argues against its own candidate in writing. A fit report with no gaps is not trustworthy.

decisions.decision: One model provider was a single point of failure
decisions.tradeoff: OpenRouter withdrew the free model this site ran on and the AI went down until it was noticed. Five free models failed five different ways in one afternoon: withdrawn, rate limited, upstream overloaded, restricted to other clients, and answering 200 then 503 a minute later. The fix was a chain across four providers with a circuit breaker rather than a better single provider. Writing it surfaced a subtler bug: the first version treated any 4xx as fatal, which is wrong, because Google answers 400 to a bad API key and Groq answers 413 to a prompt Cerebras accepts. A sabotage test caught it before it shipped.

decisions.decision: The prompt is sized to the provider
decisions.tradeoff: Groq's free tier allows 8,000 tokens a minute against a full prompt of about 10,000, so it is sent a lean knowledge base measured at 5,993 tokens against its own tokenizer. A fallback answers with less depth on project internals. A thinner answer beats no answer.

decisions.decision: The model routes are rate limited
decisions.tradeoff: Two public endpoints on a free-tier key are an open proxy for anyone who finds them, so both are capped per visitor and per day. A genuinely curious visitor can hit a wall, and the figures and notes all still work without the AI.

shipped: Grounded chat with structured UI actions, validated against known ids before the client runs them
Job-description fit check with cited matches, transferable experience and explicit gaps
Four-provider failover chain with a five-minute circuit breaker and per-attempt timeouts
Per-provider knowledge-base tiers, so a small token budget gets a prompt built to fit it
An offline provider benchmark that races the real dataset and reports latency, success rate and JSON compliance
Rate limiting on both model routes, with the daily budget split between them
Two renditions of one world, keyboard access to every figure, and a reduced-motion path
roadmap: Hybrid retrieval over the same JSON, so a question retrieves what it needs instead of sending the whole dataset every time
A labelled question set and a scoring harness, so retrieval quality is measured rather than asserted
Per-project OG images for the case studies
openQuestions: Rate-limit counters live in the running instance, so the daily cap is a brake rather than a guarantee if the platform runs several. Is a shared store worth the dependency at this size?
There is no conversation memory. Should a visitor be able to pick up where they left off, or is a stateless agent the more honest demonstration?
Voice quality is whatever the browser ships, which varies a lot by platform.
A free provider can withdraw a model at any time. The chain turns that into a slower answer instead of an outage, but it does not remove it.
whatItShows: Grounding and refusal: answers derive from a dataset, and the agent says when the dataset does not cover the question
Structured outputs treated as untrusted: every UI action is validated against known ids before it runs, and the job description is data, never instructions
Operating on infrastructure you do not control: failover, circuit breaking, prompt budgets per provider, and a benchmark to decide the order
Honesty as a product decision: statuses that do not overclaim, and a fit report that reports its own gaps

projects.name: SignalRoom
projects.statusLabel: Working demo with a published evaluation, synthetic data only
projects.tagline: A discovery transcript becomes a solution brief where every claim is tied to a line the customer said, a critic lists what could not be supported, and a human approves.
projects.idea: SignalRoom does the part of solutioning an LLM can do, extracting requirements and drafting a first brief, and makes the part it cannot be trusted with visible: what was invented, what was disputed, and what is still unknown.
projects.problem: After a discovery call a solution engineer has to turn forty minutes of messy conversation into a brief a delivery team can act on. The dangerous failure is not a missing requirement but a confident sentence nobody said: an agreed duration that was never agreed, a number lifted from a vendor sheet, a requirement that was one person thinking aloud while another disagreed.
projects.question: How do you let a model draft the brief while making it structurally unable to claim more than the conversation supports?
corePromise: Every requirement carries a quote that code verified is a verbatim substring of a numbered transcript line.
Numbers the customer never said are flagged by provenance, not silently accepted.
A vague follow-up answer cannot close an open item, whatever the model concludes.
Approval is a real interrupt in the workflow, recorded with a reviewer decision.

principles.title: Evidence before recommendation
principles.text: A claim without a quoted line is a question, not a requirement.

principles.title: Show what the model was not allowed to say
principles.text: Dropped quotes, stripped citations and flagged numbers stay visible in the room and in the eval.

principles.title: Workflow activity is inspectable, not theatrical
principles.text: Every stage does real work or does not exist; the trace shows real checkpoints.

principles.title: Works without secrets
principles.text: Recorded model runs replay the demo and the evaluation in CI with no key.

principles.title: Synthetic by rule
principles.text: Every organization, transcript and number is invented and labelled; nothing derives from a real engagement.

notList: A chat assistant with a persona
A dashboard of KPIs about the sales pipeline
A source of pricing or ROI claims
A production system or a claim of customer use

coreFlow.text: Deterministic segmentation of the transcript into numbered, speaker-attributed lines.
Structured model output; code verifies each quote against its cited line, repairs quotes found on another line, drops the rest, and records both.
SQLite full-text search over a synthetic pattern library; passages carry stable ids the brief can cite.
A brief in the working shape of a solution architecture spec; code strips citations that were not retrieved and classifies every number as customer-stated, reference-derived or invented.
Model findings merged with code findings: dropped evidence, unverified numbers, invalid citations, unaddressed contradictions, figures one speaker corrects on the next line.
A LangGraph interrupt. Approve ends the graph; request changes returns to design with the note; follow-up answers become new attributed lines and return to extract.

states.name: Awaiting review
states.text: The graph is paused at the gate with a brief, a verdict and open items.

states.name: Needs changes
states.text: The critic found a high-severity issue; the primary action becomes a change request with a note.

states.name: Approved
states.text: The graph reached its end; reviewer, timestamp and brief revision are in the audit trail.

states.name: No model
states.text: Without a key, recorded rooms open and the composer says plainly that new transcripts need one.

decisions.decision: Code gates over prompt instructions
decisions.tradeoff: Prompts are requests. Every claim, citation and number is checked in code, and the checks needed tuning before they were fair: the first live run tripped on number words and Unicode hyphens, and a later replay showed six of sixteen number findings were passage citation ids such as operational-alert-design#5 read as figures. The gate fired zero times on real runs and is kept anyway.

decisions.decision: A real LangGraph with the gate as an interrupt
decisions.tradeoff: A plain pipeline would be shorter and equally honest, but the workflow genuinely pauses with three exits and resumes after a restart. The original build had pass-through nodes; those were removed rather than kept as decoration.

decisions.decision: SQLite FTS5 instead of a vector database
decisions.tradeoff: A few dozen passages do not justify Qdrant. The previous hash embeddings scored 'alert' and 'alerts' at zero similarity. BM25 with stemming and a two-shared-terms floor is honest at this scale, behind an interface embeddings can replace.

decisions.decision: Record and replay model calls by content hash
decisions.tradeoff: Recordings are committed, so CI and the demo need no key and anyone can read which prompt produced which output. A prompt change moves the hash, so only changed stages re-record.

decisions.decision: Publish the failures with the scores
decisions.tradeoff: The model caught 3 of 8 contradictions and every room came back needing changes; both are in the README, with the miss a later code check still leaves: a gateway that is 'staying' and then proposed for replacement nineteen lines later, with no figure to compare. When a replay showed the write-up had overclaimed (padded durations flagged in every room, when one room padded them and the check passed it), the decision log was corrected in place with a date. Unmatched extractions count against precision rather than being relabelled.

stack: FastAPI
LangGraph with a SQLite checkpointer
Pydantic strict-schema structured output over an OpenAI-compatible client (Groq default, OpenRouter tested)
SQLite FTS5
React 19 and Vite
pytest (56 tests) and an evaluation runner replayed in CI

modules.name: workflow.py
modules.role: The graph: discover, extract, retrieve, design, critique, gate; state as plain dicts; projection to a Room.

modules.name: grounding.py
modules.role: The code gates: quote verification and repair, number provenance, citation stripping, the non-answer rule, question similarity, figure corrections between consecutive speakers.

modules.name: model_client.py
modules.role: structured_call: strict JSON schema output, recording and replay by content hash, latency, tokens and cost per call, and which provider served each live call.

modules.name: retrieval.py
modules.role: FTS5 pattern library with stable passage ids.

modules.name: evals/
modules.role: Ten synthetic fixtures with gold rubrics and planted traps, the scoring module, the runner that writes results and the docs block.

architecture.dataModel: Room = utterances[line, speaker, text] + requirements[id, evidence{line, speaker, quote}] + open_items[status, answered_line, rejected_answers] + brief{snapshot, readiness, constraints, phases, success_measures, risks} + critique{findings[kind, severity, source]} + grounding{proposed, passed, repaired, dropped} + metrics
keyIdeas: The speaker on every quote comes from the transcript, never from the model.
Numbers are classified by provenance: said by the customer (number words folded to digits), present only in reference material, or nowhere.
A follow-up answer becomes a new attributed line, so re-extraction sees it as evidence; the code refuses to let a non-answer resolve anything.
The evaluation plants traps: injection lines, numbers seeded in the reference library, speaker contradictions, deliberate gaps.

projects.whereAIFits: Three model calls per room: extract, design, critique, each with strict structured output. The model proposes; code decides what survives. The interesting part is not the prompts but the gates around them and the evaluation that shows where the model still fails: it treats a correction between speakers as resolved rather than disputed, which a code check now catches when the correction is a figure on the next line, and it writes numbers nobody stated, mostly exit-criteria targets, which the number check flags in six of ten rooms.
projects.process: Started from a Codex scaffold that was audited first (AUDIT.md): keyword extraction dressed as an agent, pass-through graph nodes, evals that could not fail. Rebuilt in ordered commits with Claude: retrieval, model client, the real graph, fixtures, the evaluation harness, a first live run, and check tuning from what that run exposed. Design followed the Impeccable process: product record, a direction round with alternates, a written direction contract, a fresh-context finish review, and DESIGN.md recorded from the built code.
shipped: Six-stage workflow with a human gate as a LangGraph interrupt
Code-enforced quote verification with repairs and drops recorded
Number provenance check across the whole brief
Follow-up loop where non-answers cannot close items
Ten synthetic fixtures, scoring harness, CI replay from committed recordings

A published evaluation of run 1 on ten fixtures: 0.95 requirement recall, 0.87 precision, 119 of 119 model quotes passing the verbatim check, 4 of 4 injection lines ignored, 2 of 2 planted numbers kept out, and 3 of 8 contradictions caught by the model. Replaying run 1's recorded outputs through a figure-correction check added later gives 7 of 8, but that check was written after seeing those misses and is scored on the same fixtures, and run 2's revised prompts are unrecorded because the provider account has no credit.
Code check for a figure one speaker corrects on the next line, kept as a dispute rather than a resolved value; on the ten transcripts it fires on four pairs and nowhere else
Recorded rooms that open with no key
DOCX export of the brief
Read-only MCP tools over search, rooms and evaluation results
roadmap: Run 2 of the evaluation with the revised contradiction and duration prompts (written, unrecorded: the provider account has no credit)
Streaming stage updates in the UI instead of a synchronous run
Run the figure-correction check before the brief is drafted, so the brief can address what it finds
More fixtures before quoting rates with confidence
openQuestions: Figure corrections are now kept as a dispute rather than a resolved value. Can a reversal with no figures, a fact and its contradiction far apart, be caught without leaving it to the model?
How much of the brief should the model be allowed to write before the reviewer has confirmed the open items?
Is a single accountable reviewer the right gate, or does a delivery lead need a second one?
whatItShows: AI engineering: structured output, grounding enforced in code, prompt-injection surface treated as data, recorded and replayable model calls
Evaluation discipline: labelled synthetic fixtures with traps, scores published with their failures, regression floors in CI
Solutioning judgment: the brief has the shape a delivery team actually needs, with open items owned and unknowns kept visible
Proportionate architecture: FTS5 over a vector database, one graph library where it earns its keep, decisions written down with their alternatives
Honesty as a product rule: synthetic data only, no production claims, the audit of the original build committed alongside the rebuild
